theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of planning organisational needs in a public body?
options: To decide which officers will be promoted this year
To match resources to the services planned
To write the agency's mission and vision statements
To plan the yearly staff party and sports day

questions.stem: Andrea Bailey must plan her agency's needs for the next three years. Which documents should she start from?
options: Last year's budget for staff social events
The newest catalogue from the office supplier
The staff list sorted by date of joining
The agency's strategic and business plans

questions.stem: Which list best covers the main types of organisational need?
options: People, skills, premises, equipment, ICT and money
Staff numbers only, as people are the main cost
Computers, printers and other office machines only
Office furniture and stationery only

questions.stem: A ministry wants to forecast demand for its services over five years. Which tool helps it review political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors?
options: A Gantt chart
A fishbone diagram
A PESTLE analysis
A RACI chart

questions.stem: A parish office handled 20,000 applications last year. Demand is expected to grow by 10% a year. About how many should it plan for in two years' time?
Each processing officer can handle about 1,500 applications a year. Demand next year is forecast at 33,000. How many officers are needed?
An agency needs 22 officers next year. It has 18 now, and 2 of them will retire before then. What is the staffing gap?
Before asking for new equipment, why should a manager prepare an inventory of the assets the unit already has?
options: To find old items that can be sold cheaply to staff
To make the request look bigger and more urgent
To see what can be reused before buying new
To give the internal auditors something to check

questions.stem: What does a gap analysis compare in needs planning?
options: Last year's budget with this year's budget only
Staff salaries with salaries in similar private firms
The number of men and women on staff
The resources needed with the resources available

questions.stem: Why should the planning officer ask each unit head to submit its needs with evidence, rather than guessing them herself?
options: So unit heads can ask for whatever they like
So the plan reflects real workloads and gaps
So the planning officer can avoid any analysis
So the plan can be finished without a deadline

questions.stem: Unit requests add up to J$85 million, but only J$60 million is likely to be available. What should the planning officer do?
options: Rank needs by legal duty, risk and service impact
Cut every unit's request by exactly the same percentage
Fund the requests in the order in which they arrived

questions.stem: Unit requests total J$85 million and J$60 million is available. About what percentage of the requests can be funded?
Which need should usually rank highest in a needs plan?
options: New padded chairs for the board meeting room
A larger, brighter sign for the staff car park
Bigger screens for staff who would like them
Fire equipment that the law requires

questions.stem: An agency needs extra office space for 15 staff for two years while a new building is finished. Which option is likely to give best value?
options: Lease suitable space for the two years
Buy a large building for the long term
Build a new office on rented land
Squeeze the staff into the existing corridor

questions.stem: When comparing two photocopiers, why should the officer look at whole-life cost, not only the purchase price?
options: Because the cheaper one is always the better buy
Because running costs can exceed the price
Because the law fixes the price of every copier
Because suppliers prefer to sell on that basis

questions.stem: Copier A costs J$600,000 and J$90,000 a year to run. Copier B costs J$450,000 and J$140,000 a year to run. Over five years, which costs less in total, and by how much?
Two agencies in the same town each want a new conference room that each would use about once a week. Which option should the planners consider first?
options: Each builds its own room
Both hire hotel rooms every week
Neither holds meetings
Share one room under a written agreement

questions.stem: When might outsourcing a service, such as cleaning, best meet an organisation's needs?
options: When a contractor meets standards at lower cost
When managers want to hand over all responsibility
Whenever staff in the unit ask for it to happen
Never, because public bodies may not outsource

questions.stem: A ministry plans to move most of its services online within three years. Which need is most likely to rise?
options: More filing cabinets for paper application forms
ICT systems, data security and digital skills
More counter space and seating for long queues
A larger supply of postage stamps and envelopes

questions.stem: A new law gives an agency inspection duties it has never had before. Which need should the plan identify?
options: More parking spaces for visitors to the head office
A new logo and colour scheme for the agency
Trained inspectors with the right equipment
Longer lunch breaks for the existing office staff

questions.stem: What must a business case for a new fleet of vehicles include?
options: The preferred colour and model of each vehicle
The names and addresses of each driver's family
A promise that no vehicle will ever break down
Need, options, costs, benefits and risks

questions.stem: Why should needs planning be finished in time for the organisation's budget preparation?
options: So that agreed needs can be included in the budget request
So that the budget can be ignored
So that planners can take leave
So that suppliers can raise prices

questions.stem: A needs plan relies on a new office opening in January. What is the best way to manage the risk of building delays?
options: Assume the builder will finish on time
Plan a fallback, such as extending the current lease, and monitor progress
Cancel the new office

questions.stem: A disaster management agency is planning for the hurricane season. Which need is most important to plan in advance?
options: Extra office plants for reception
New uniforms for the annual parade
Emergency supplies, standby staff rosters and back-up power
A new website colour scheme

questions.stem: A unit head claims her team needs eight more officers but gives no workload figures. What should the planning officer do?
options: Approve all eight at once
Refuse without discussion
Halve the request
Ask for workload data and test the claim

questions.stem: Which groups should be consulted when planning the needs of a new public health clinic?
options: Staff, the local community and the facilities unit
Only the architect who will design the building
Only the Minister's office, which approves funds
Only the firm supplying the medical equipment

questions.stem: An agency will need 6 extra laptops at J$145,000 each and 2 printers at J$85,000 each. What is the total cost?
Six new officers will each cost J$3,200,000 a year, including allowances. What will they cost in a full year?
Six new officers, each costing J$3,200,000 a year, will start on 1 October. The financial year ends on 31 March. What will they cost in this financial year?
A unit of 40 staff will grow to 52. The office allows about 8 m² per workstation. How much extra floor space is needed for the new workstations?
options: 416 m²
320 m²
120 m²

questions.stem: When planning a new customer service centre, why should the needs plan include access for people with disabilities?
options: Because most users of public services have disabilities
Because services must be open to everyone

Because ramps always cost less than building steps

questions.stem: Which of these is an information need in an organisational needs plan?
options: A new staff canteen
Extra security guards

questions.stem: Halfway through the year, demand is 15% higher than forecast. What should the planning officer do?
options: Review the plan and adjust priorities or resources
Wait and deal with it in next year's plan
Keep the figures quiet so no one is worried
Ask staff to work unpaid every weekend

questions.stem: Why should a needs plan state the assumptions behind its forecasts?
options: So that the plan looks longer and more detailed
So that no one is able to question the figures
So that the figures can never be changed later
So they can be checked and updated if needed

questions.stem: Which statement best describes value for money when meeting a need?
options: Always choosing the cheapest item on offer
Best mix of quality, life cost and fitness
Always choosing the most expensive item on offer
Spending all the budget before the year ends

questions.stem: One unit's workload has fallen since services moved online, while another's has grown. Which option should be considered before recruiting?
options: Close both units and start again from scratch
Recruit new staff for both units at the same time
Retrain and move staff from the quieter unit

questions.stem: When planning new vehicles, a public body wants to cut fuel costs and emissions. Which step helps most?
options: Compare fuel-efficient and electric models on whole-life cost
Buy the largest and most powerful vehicles available
Keep all the old vehicles running for as long as possible
Choose the vehicles mainly by their colour and style

questions.stem: A draft needs plan proposes closing a small office, but no decision has been made. How should the planning officer treat the draft?
options: Post it on social media for comment
Tell the office staff informally
Share it with suppliers
Keep it confidential until it is approved for release

questions.stem: An agency's objective is to cut waiting times for permits from 20 days to 10. Which need does this objective best support?
options: A new sofa and coffee table for reception
Extra processing staff and online tracking
A staff choir to raise morale at year end
A larger car park for both staff and visitors

questions.stem: Which method sorts needs into "must have", "should have", "could have" and "won't have this time"?
options: SWOT
PESTLE
MoSCoW
RACI

questions.stem: A new scanning system costing J$2,400,000 will save J$800,000 a year in staff time and storage. What is the simple payback period?
options: 3 years
2 years
4 years
8 years

questions.stem: How often should an organisational needs plan normally be reviewed?
options: Only when the Minister changes
Once every ten years
Only after an audit finding
At least yearly, and when major changes occur

questions.stem: Which units should the planning officer work with most closely to cost staffing and equipment needs?
options: The canteen manager
The finance and HR units
The security staff on the night shift
The visitors' book

questions.stem: A needs plan for a new office fit-out totals J$12,000,000. The agency adds a 10% contingency. What is the total with contingency?
A unit head inflates her needs request, expecting it to be cut. What is the main problem with this?
options: It distorts priorities and starves real needs
There is no problem; it is a smart way to get funds
It saves the planning officer time in the end
It makes the final plan more accurate overall

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Each inspector can complete about 400 inspections a year. The plan forecasts 9,200 inspections. How many inspectors are needed?
Demand of 15,000 cases a year is forecast to grow by 20%. How many cases should be planned for?
What one-word term names moving existing staff from one unit to another where they are more needed?
What one-word term names the extra amount, often a percentage, added to a cost estimate to cover costs that cannot be foreseen?
A new post costs J$2,400,000 a year and is filled with 3 months of the financial year left. What will it cost in this financial year, in J$?
What one-word term names the amount of work, such as cases or applications, that a unit must handle in a period?
A records scanning system will cost J$3,000,000 and should save J$750,000 each year in storage and staff time. After how many years will the savings repay the cost?
What one-word term names paying an outside firm to provide a service, such as security, instead of using the organisation's own staff?
What one word describes a forecast that carries past figures forward, such as "cases rose 5% a year, so expect 5% more"? (It may be followed by "analysis".)
A unit needs 15 extra workstations at about 8 m² each. How many square metres of extra space does it need?
What three-word term names the plan for keeping key services running during and after a disaster such as a hurricane?
Twelve desks are needed at J$38,500 each. What is the total cost, in J$?
What one-word term names the most work an organisation can handle with its present staff and equipment?
A unit has 30 staff and needs 36. By what percentage must its staffing rise?
What one word names the final stage of an asset's life, when an old vehicle or computer is sold, recycled or scrapped?

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to plan the organisational needs of a government agency for the next three years.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the agency's strategic and business plans, because needs exist to deliver its objectives and services. Next I would scan the environment, for example with a PESTLE analysis, to forecast changes in demand, such as population growth, new laws or a move to online services. I would then forecast workload for each service using past trends and known changes, and state the assumptions. Alongside this I would assess current capacity: staff numbers and skills, accommodation, vehicles, ICT, equipment and its condition, and the budget. Comparing need with what exists gives a gap analysis for each type of resource. I would ask unit heads to confirm the gaps with evidence and consult finance, HR and facilities. For each gap I would look at options, such as redeploying staff, sharing space, leasing or buying, and cost them on a whole-life basis. Needs would be ranked against agreed criteria such as legal duty, risk and service impact. The result would be a costed needs plan, approved by senior management in time for the budget, and then monitored and reviewed each year.
markingPoints: Links needs to the strategic and business plans
Scans the environment and forecasts demand with stated assumptions
Assesses current capacity and identifies gaps
Considers and costs options, consulting other units
Prioritises, gets approval in time for the budget and reviews yearly

essays.stem: A tax office processed 48,000 returns last year with 32 officers. Demand is forecast to rise by 25% over the next two years, while a new online system is expected to raise each officer's output by 20%. Work out how many officers will be needed and the effect on staffing, and comment on the assumptions.
essays.modelAnswer: Each officer now processes 48,000 ÷ 32 = 1,500 returns a year. Demand in two years will be 48,000 × 1.25 = 60,000 returns. With the online system, each officer's output rises to 1,500 × 1.2 = 1,800 returns. Officers needed = 60,000 ÷ 1,800 = 33.3, which must be rounded up to 34, because 33 officers could handle only 59,400 returns while 34 can handle 61,200. The office therefore needs 2 more officers than the 32 it has, not the 8 it would need without the system (60,000 ÷ 1,500 = 40). These results depend on assumptions. The 25% growth may be wrong if the economy or tax rules change. The 20% gain assumes the system is delivered on time, works well and that staff are trained; such gains often take months to appear. Retirements or leave could reduce the number of officers available. I would therefore state these assumptions in the plan, recruit the 2 extra officers, prepare a fallback in case the system is late, such as temporary staff, and review the forecast every six months.
markingPoints: Calculates output per officer (1,500) and future demand (60,000)
Calculates new output (1,800) and officers needed (34, rounded up), a gap of 2
Compares with 40 officers needed without the system
Comments on the growth, system and staff availability assumptions
Recommends a fallback and regular review

essays.stem: Unit requests for next year total J$120 million, but the likely budget is J$90 million. Explain how you would prioritise the needs, and justify your method.
essays.modelAnswer: The budget covers J$90 million of J$120 million, or 75%, leaving a shortfall of J$30 million, or 25% of the requests. Cutting every request by 25% would be simple but unfair, because it would cut essential and minor needs alike. Instead, I would agree clear criteria with senior management before looking at the requests: legal and safety duties, link to the strategic objectives, effect on services to the public, risk if the need is not met, value for money and readiness to proceed. Each criterion would be given a weight, and each request would be scored by a small panel, using the evidence the units submitted. I would first check the requests themselves, removing any that lack evidence and looking for cheaper options such as sharing or redeploying. Needs that the law requires would be funded first. The rest would be ranked by score and funded until the J$90 million is reached, with the next items kept on a reserve list in case savings or extra money arise. I would explain the results to unit heads. This method is transparent, consistent and focused on the agency's purpose.
markingPoints: Calculates 75% funded and the J$30 million (25%) shortfall
Explains why equal cuts are unfair
Sets weighted criteria such as legal duty, objectives, service impact, risk and value
Tests requests for evidence and cheaper options; funds legal duties first
Ranks, keeps a reserve list and explains decisions transparently

essays.stem: An agency's 60 staff will grow to 80 within two years, and its office is already full. Compare leasing more space, building, sharing with another public body and remote working, and recommend an approach.
essays.modelAnswer: Leasing extra space is quick and flexible, and avoids a large capital cost, but rent is a lasting expense and a second site may split teams. Building gives space that exactly fits the agency and may be cheapest over many years, but it needs a large capital budget, takes years to plan and build, and so cannot meet a two-year need. Sharing with another public body that has spare space makes good use of public assets and may be cheap, but depends on that body's plans and needs a clear agreement on costs, security and access. Remote or hybrid working could reduce the number of desks needed, for example if staff rotate days in the office, but it needs laptops, secure systems, a policy and good supervision, and suits only some jobs; counter staff must be on site. I would recommend combining options: introduce hybrid working for suitable roles to free about a quarter of desks, and seek shared or leased space nearby for the remainder, on a lease no longer than needed. Building should be considered only in the long-term plan, if growth continues.
markingPoints: Evaluates leasing with a strength and a limit
Evaluates building, including timing and capital cost
Evaluates sharing with another public body
Evaluates remote or hybrid working and its needs
Makes a justified recommendation that fits the two-year need

essays.stem: Vehicle A costs J$6,500,000 and J$600,000 a year to run; Vehicle B costs J$5,200,000 and J$950,000 a year to run. Using a six-year life, compare their whole-life costs and explain why whole-life cost and value for money matter when planning needs.
essays.modelAnswer: Over six years, Vehicle A costs J$6,500,000 + (6 × J$600,000) = J$6,500,000 + J$3,600,000 = J$10,100,000. Vehicle B costs J$5,200,000 + (6 × J$950,000) = J$5,200,000 + J$5,700,000 = J$10,900,000. Vehicle A is cheaper over its life by J$800,000, although it costs J$1,300,000 more to buy. Checking: J$10,900,000 − J$10,100,000 = J$800,000. This shows why whole-life cost matters: the purchase price is only part of the cost. Fuel, servicing, insurance, repairs, training and disposal can add more than the price over the years, so a cheap item can be the expensive choice. Value for money means the best mix of whole-life cost, quality and fitness for the job, not simply the lowest price. Public bodies spend public money and must be able to show that they chose wisely. In this case I would also check reliability, the availability of parts and service in rural parishes, fuel use and emissions, and the expected resale value, before recommending Vehicle A.
markingPoints: Calculates Vehicle A J$10,100,000 and Vehicle B J$10,900,000
Identifies A as cheaper by J$800,000 despite the higher price, with a check
Explains that running and disposal costs can outweigh the price
Defines value for money as cost, quality and fitness for purpose
Links to accountability for public money and lists other factors to check

essays.stem: Explain how you would gather and test needs from unit managers, staff and service users, so that an agency's needs plan is based on evidence rather than opinion.
essays.modelAnswer: I would issue a simple template to unit managers asking for each need, its link to an objective, the evidence (workload figures, waiting times, asset condition, incidents), the options considered, the cost and the risk if it is not met. I would set a deadline and offer a short briefing so managers understand what good evidence looks like. I would check managers' figures against data held centrally, such as case-management reports, the asset register, maintenance logs and HR records. Staff are often closest to the problems, so I would hold short focus groups or a survey to ask what slows their work and what they lack. Service users could be asked through customer surveys, complaint records and, for a new service, community meetings, to show where demand is rising or service falls short. I would visit a sample of offices to see conditions for myself. Where claims and data disagree, I would discuss them with the manager. Finally, the evidence for each need would be recorded in the plan, so that decision-makers can see why each need was included and ranked as it was.
markingPoints: Uses a standard template requiring evidence from managers
Checks claims against central data and records
Gathers staff views through focus groups or surveys
Uses service-user evidence such as surveys and complaints
Tests disagreements, visits sites and records the evidence in the plan

essays.stem: Use a PESTLE analysis to explain the factors a municipal corporation should consider when planning its needs for markets and solid waste services over the next five years.
essays.modelAnswer: Political factors include national and local priorities, such as plans to modernise town centres, and changes after local elections that may shift funding. Economic factors include growth or decline in trade and tourism, which affect the number of vendors and the amount of waste, as well as fuel and equipment prices and the corporation's own income from fees. Social factors include population growth in new housing schemes, changing shopping habits and public expectations of clean, safe markets. Technological factors include new collection vehicles, route-planning software, cashless fee payment and recycling methods, which may change the staff and equipment needed. Legal factors include public health and environmental laws, the rules on waste disposal and procurement rules for public bodies, all of which set standards that must be planned for. Environmental factors include hurricanes and flooding, which can damage markets and create sudden waste, and pressure to reduce landfill and plastic. From this analysis the corporation can forecast demand, identify new needs, such as more trucks for new housing areas or drainage at markets, and plan contingencies for storms.
markingPoints: Gives relevant political and economic factors
Gives relevant social and technological factors
Gives relevant legal factors by general purpose
Gives relevant environmental factors, including hurricanes
Links the analysis to forecasting specific needs and contingencies

essays.stem: Prepare the outline of a business case for a new case-management system for a public agency, explaining what each section must show.
essays.modelAnswer: The business case would open with a short summary of the need, the recommended option, its cost and the decision required. The strategic case would explain the need: for example, paper files cause delays, lost documents and complaints, and the agency's plan aims to halve processing times. It would link the system to that objective and to national digital policy. The options section would compare at least three options, such as doing nothing, improving the paper system with more staff, and buying a new system, against agreed criteria. The economic and financial section would set out the whole-life costs of each option, including licences, hardware, training, support and data migration, and the benefits, such as staff time saved, and show payback and affordability within the budget. The risks section would list the main risks, such as delays, data loss or staff resistance, with responses. The delivery section would explain how the project would be bought under the procurement rules for public bodies, the timetable, the project team and how benefits will be measured. It would end with a clear recommendation.
markingPoints: Includes a summary and the decision required
Explains the need and links it to objectives
Compares realistic options, including doing nothing
Shows whole-life costs, benefits, payback and affordability
Covers risks, procurement, delivery and benefit measurement, ending with a recommendation

essays.stem: Explain how risk and uncertainty should be handled in an organisational needs plan, with examples involving hurricanes, project delays and changes in demand.
essays.modelAnswer: No forecast is certain, so a needs plan should state its assumptions and identify the main risks to it. For each risk, the planner should judge how likely it is and how serious the effect would be, and plan a response. Hurricanes are a known seasonal risk in Jamaica. The plan should include back-up power, protected records and ICT, emergency supplies, a business continuity plan and a contingency budget for repairs, and avoid scheduling critical moves or installations at the height of the season. Project delays, such as a late new building or ICT system, can be handled by allowing time in the schedule, monitoring progress monthly and having a fallback, for example extending a lease or keeping the old system running. Changes in demand can be handled by forecasting a range, such as low, likely and high, rather than a single figure, and by choosing flexible options such as temporary staff, leasing or shared space, which can be scaled up or down. A contingency of perhaps 5% to 10% of costs may be added, as the agency's rules allow. The risks should be reviewed regularly and the plan updated.
markingPoints: States assumptions and assesses likelihood and impact
Plans for hurricanes with continuity measures and timing
Handles delays with time allowances, monitoring and fallbacks
Handles demand changes with ranges and flexible options
Uses contingency and regular review

essays.stem: Explain how you would monitor and review an agency's needs plan during the year and report on it to senior management.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set up a simple tracker listing each approved need, its owner, the budget, the target date and the measure that shows it has been met, for example "six officers in post by 1 October" or "new vehicles in use in the western region". Each month, owners would update progress, spending and any problems. I would also track the key demand figures behind the plan, such as applications received and waiting times, against the forecast, because the plan may need to change if demand differs. Every quarter I would prepare a short report for senior management, using red, amber and green ratings, showing needs on track, at risk and late, spending against budget, changes in demand and any new needs, with recommendations, such as moving money from a delayed item to an urgent one, within the financial rules. I would meet unit heads to discuss problems early. At year end, I would review what was achieved, whether the needs met turned into better services, and what was learned about forecasting, and use this to prepare the next year's plan.
markingPoints: Uses a tracker with owners, budgets, dates and measures
Collects regular progress and spending updates
Monitors demand against the forecast
Reports quarterly with ratings, issues and recommendations within the rules
Reviews results at year end and feeds lessons into the next plan

practical1.title: Prepare an organisational needs analysis and costed needs plan
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for a made-up public body, such as a parish permit office, an agency's regional office or a public clinic. The pack includes its objectives for the next three years, workload figures for the last three years, the staff list with planned retirements, an inventory of vehicles, computers and furniture with their condition, the floor space, a price list in J$ and a likely budget. As a group, prepare a needs plan pack containing: a demand forecast on a spreadsheet with the assumptions stated; a capacity and gap analysis for staff, space, equipment and ICT; a one-page PESTLE summary; a list of needs ranked against agreed criteria (for example legal duty, link to objectives, risk and value for money); a costed needs plan within the budget, with a contingency and every sum checked twice; and a short note of the main risks. Give each member a named role: plan lead (keeps time, agrees the ranking criteria and assembles the pack), demand analyst (prepares the forecast), resources analyst (prepares the capacity and gap analysis), cost officer (costs the plan and checks the sums), and risk and environment officer (writes the PESTLE summary and risk note). In a group of four, the plan lead also writes the risk note. At the end, each member explains their part to the assessor in two minutes.
materials: Data pack, price list and budget from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
photos: The flipchart with roles, timetable and the agreed ranking criteria
The demand forecast on screen, with the assumptions shown
The ranked list of needs with scores
The costed needs plan with contingency and the second check marked
The PESTLE summary, risk note and assembled pack
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the pack
Forecast uses the data correctly and states its assumptions
Gaps are worked out correctly for each type of resource
Needs are ranked against clear criteria, with legal duties first
Plan is within the budget, includes a contingency and was checked twice
Options such as reuse, sharing or redeployment were considered before buying
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up public body and data; treat the pack as confidential
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Listen to every member's ideas respectfully and share the work fairly
Take short breaks and keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Prepare and present a business case for a priority need
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a priority need from a made-up public body and three options to meet it, with costs in J$ over five years, for example: replace six old vehicles (buy new, lease, or repair and keep), or deal with a backlog of applications (hire temporary staff, buy a case-management system, or share staff with another office). As a group, prepare a business case of no more than three pages: the need and its link to the body's objectives; the three options compared on whole-life cost over five years, benefits, payback where it applies, and risks (every sum checked twice); and a justified recommendation. Then present the business case in 10 minutes to a senior management panel played by the assessor and one or two other trainees, using four to six slides or a flipchart, and answer the panel's questions. One member records the panel's decision and actions as minutes. Give each member a named role: case lead (writes the need and recommendation and opens the presentation), cost analyst (works the whole-life costs and payback), benefits and risk officer (compares benefits and risks), presenter (prepares and presents the slides with the lead), and minute-taker (records the questions, decision and actions). In a group of four, the case lead also presents the slides. Every member must speak in the presentation or answer a question.
materials: Priority need, options and cost data from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet, word-processing and presentation software, and a printer
photos: The whole-life cost comparison with the second check marked
The slides or flipchart used in the presentation
The presentation to the panel in progress (slides only if anyone prefers no photo)
The minutes showing the panel's questions, decision and actions
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Whole-life costs and payback are correct and were checked twice
Options are compared fairly on cost, benefits and risks
Recommendation follows from the evidence and links to the body's objectives
Spoke clearly in the presentation or answered a question accurately
Minutes record the decision and actions with owners and dates
safety: Treat the data as confidential and use only the made-up names and figures
Speak respectfully to the panel and to each other, and let each person finish
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph slides and notes if a person prefers
Share the workload fairly and take a short break between preparing and presenting
